questions.text:
In a directed acyclic graph with a source vertex s, the quality-score of a directed path is defined to be the product of the weights of the edges on the path. Further, for a vertex v other than s, the quality-score of v is defined to be the maximum among the quality-scores of all the paths from s to v. The quality-score of s is assumed to be 1.

The sum of the quality-scores of all vertices on the graph shown above is ______
questions.solution:
Go in topological order, taking the best product into each vertex:
- s = 1, c = 1, a = 9
- f = c [latex]\times[/latex] 9 = 9, b = a [latex]\times[/latex] 1 = 9
- d = max(c [latex]\times[/latex] 1, a [latex]\times[/latex] 1) = 9
- g = max(f [latex]\times[/latex] 1, d [latex]\times[/latex] 9) = 81
- e = max(d [latex]\times[/latex] 9, b [latex]\times[/latex] 1) = 81
- t = max(g [latex]\times[/latex] 1, e [latex]\times[/latex] 9) = 729

Sum = 1 + 1 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 81 + 81 + 729 = 929

Answer: 929

questions.text: Let S be a set of consisting of 10 elements. The number of tuples of the form (A,B) such that A and B are subsets of S, and [latex]A\subseteq B[/latex] is _______
questions.solution:
For [latex]A\subseteq B\subseteq S[/latex], each element of S is in one of 3 states: not in B, in B but not A, or in A.

[latex]3^{10}=59049[/latex]

Answer: 59049

questions.text:
Consider the following directed graph:

Which of the following is/are correct about the graph?
questions.solution:
Following the arrows, the graph has three directed cycles:
- around the top-middle square (between the top two rows),
- around the bottom-left square through S,
- around the bottom-right square.

- A cycle means there is no topological order [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- A DFS from S reaches every vertex, and each of these three cycles produces exactly one back edge [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 back edges [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Every graph has strongly connected components (at least single vertices) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Not every pair is mutually reachable (e.g. nothing returns from the top-right corner) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

questions.text: A bag has [latex]r[/latex] red balls and [latex]b[/latex] black balls. All balls are identical except for their colours. In a trial, a ball is randomly drawn from the bag, its colour is noted and the ball is placed back into the bag along with another ball of the same colour. Note that the number of balls in the bag will increase by one, after the trial. A sequence of four such trials is conducted. Which one of the following choices gives the probability of drawing a red ball in the fourth trial?
questions.solution:
This is Polya's urn. By symmetry, every draw has the same chance of being red as the first draw.

Check for the 2nd draw: [latex]\frac{r}{r+b}\cdot\frac{r+1}{r+b+1}+\frac{b}{r+b}\cdot\frac{r}{r+b+1}=\frac{r(r+b+1)}{(r+b)(r+b+1)}=\frac{r}{r+b}[/latex]. The same holds for the 4th.

Answer: [latex]\frac{r}{r+b}[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text:
In an examination, a student can choose the order in which two questions (QuesA and QuesB) must be attempted.

If the first question is answered wrong, the student gets zero marks.
If the first question is answered correctly and the second question is not answered correctly, the student gets the marks only for the first question.
If both the questions are answered correctly, the student gets the sum of the marks of the two questions.

The following table shows the probability of correctly answering a question and the marks of the question respectively.

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{question} & \text{probabiloty of answering correctly} & \text{marks} \\ \hline \textsf{QuesA} & 0.8 & 10 \\ \textsf{QuesB} & 0.5 & 20 \end{array}[/latex]

Assuming that the student always wants to maximize her expected marks in the examination, in which order should she attempt the questions and what is the expected marks for that order (assume that the questions are independent)?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- A first: [latex]0.8\times(10+0.5\times20)=0.8\times20=16[/latex]
- B first: [latex]0.5\times(20+0.8\times10)=0.5\times28=14[/latex]

A first gives more.

Answer: First QuesA and then QuesB. Expected marks 16
